newsitem.title: FRANCE: European court hears Turkey rights cases.
newsitem.headline: European court hears Turkey rights cases.

text.p: Ankara's human rights record came under the spotlight on Wednesday as the European Court of Human Rights heard fresh allegations of torture and other abuses by the Turkish authorities in Kurdish areas.
In the latest cases to come before the court, one Turkish woman alleged she was tortured and raped while in custody while four others accused security forces of burning down houses in their village.
A decision was not expected in either proceeding for several months.

In a case heard by the court on Wednesday morning, 20-year-old Sukran Aydin from Derik, in southeastern Turkey, said she was beaten and raped while in the custody of Turkish gendarmes for three days in 1993.
Aydin, who was 16 at the time of her arrest, was never charged with any crime.

The Turkish government has denied ever detaining her. According to government lawyers, she was described in intelligence reports as a terrorist working for the separatist Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).

In the second case, heard on Wednesday afternoon, four women said that Turkish gendarmes burned down 10 to 13 homes in their southeastern village of Saggoze village in 1993 after PKK guerrillas attacked a gendarmerie station in nearby Ucdamlar.
One of the women, Sariye Uvat, also blamed the security forces for the death of her twins, born prematurely after she was expelled from her home.
The four said the gendarmes told them they were burning the houses to punish them for helping terrorists.
Attorneys for the Turkish government have denied official involvement, arguing instead that the houses were burned by members of the PKK who had taken over the village and then fled.
The court ruled last month that Turkish police had tortured a Kurd who was arrested in 1992 as a suspected terrorist but never charged.

In that case, the court ordered Ankara to pay damages and legal costs to the relatives of Zeki Aksoy, who said he had been tortured while held incommunicado for at least two weeks in a prison in southeastern Turkey.

In another case, decided in mid-September, the court ruled that Turkish security forces had violated the European Convention on Human Rights by destroying the southeastern village of Kelekci in 1992-93.

In that case, as in the case of Saggoze, Kurdish villagers charged that Turkish security forces had been taking revenge for attacks by Kurdish separatists while the Turkish authorities argued that the village had been destroyed by PKK guerrillas.
The rights court is part of the 40-nation Council of Europe, of which Turkey is a member. The council was set up after World War Two to promote democracy and human rights across Europe.
